doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

chapter: Following the drum to New York
title: Staying with Emile Latimer in Buffalo and a dream of drummers
summary: Asked about other spiritual paths, he describes living with Emile Latimer, who taught drumming as a way of life, and a dream of drummers he must meet.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I’m not sure if I can phrase this question correctly but if you had this spiritual calling, would there have been another way to pursue that call without being a percussionist? In order words could you have become a priest within that religion as opposed to following the percussion path?

I am sure. I’m sure there are people who have done it. But for me and for everybody the path is different. Right? For me it really happened in my relationship with the drum. So, and interestingly the drum that I was hearing, which I didn’t know, was batá. And I remember specifically when I went to, when I left Trinidad I went straight to Emile Latimer in Buffalo. Emile had set up a room in his house for me, I mean decorated with Africanisms all around. Listen, I came to Emile, I stayed with Emile for a month until — and Emile was not the kind of person who would sit you down and teach you, “Now the left hand is what’s doing this and the right hand is what’s doing this.” No. Emile was about being a drummer is a life experience. This is what you do because this is your soul. Emile didn’t sit down and practice. No. Emile lived that drum every single day. So every day we would get up, we would have breakfast, we would do meditation, etcetera, and we went out to work as drummers. And he carried me to every gig.
